## Composition and why

A wide, low landscape, two thirds sky. The sun has just set behind a small
town on the far edge of a flat, marshy plain by a lagoon (the Pomeranian
coast country around Greifswald that Friedrich drew all his life). The
town is only a silhouette on the horizon: a tall Gothic tower with a spire,
a second, blunter church tower, a row of roofs and trees, a windmill off to

light in the land. The meadows step down in value toward us. In the right
foreground a low dark rise with dry grass carries two small figures seen
from behind, a man and a woman, standing and looking toward the town and
the glow. A thin waxing crescent hangs above the glow, its lit limb turned
toward where the sun went down.

What it draws on (from knowledge, not pictures): the Greifswald views and
meadows (a town seen as a silhouette of towers across flat land), the
evening and moon pictures (figures from behind, a crescent near the
afterglow), the Rückenfigur as the viewer's stand-in, the great empty sky
laid thin and stippled, the low horizon, symmetry avoided but the glow as
the still center. Palette: lead white, smalt, cobalt, ochres, red earth,
vermilion (a little in the glow), umber, bone black.

p='notes/r14_p2.md'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace("""## Method, stage by stage

(written as I go)""","""## Method, stage by stage

Canvas 1000 × 714 units (aspect 1.4), Style::friedrich (Dresden grounds, 1820
palette). Horizon at 468. Every look below judged on the 2400 px render,
whole and in crops.

1. **sky** (≈95 s of the 125 s render, most of it priming). A thin dead
   color first, a step darker and duller than the sky, crossed strokes;
   dried. Then the lay-in: long near-level arcs of the broad filbert, the
   color field carrying the whole sky (warm cream at the horizon under the
   glow, a greenish cream band, a breath of violet "purple light" high over
   the sun's place, smalt/cobalt gray-blue at the top) and the cloud streaks
   in the same wet paint; a second crossing pass; the badger top to bottom;
   a coarse stipple into the wet whose every dip moves only 45% from what is
   there toward the sky wanted; dried; a fine stipple barely lighter than
   the field (+0.012 L), denser toward the glow.
2. **moon**: a young crescent, lit limb turned toward where the sun set
   (below left), horns up-right. A mask (disc minus offset disc) worked with
   short strokes of a small round along the limb, clipped.
3. **far**: the far shore as a pale level strip (small round, level strokes)
   and upright hatching only where it rises into far woods; the town as one
   cool gray-violet backlit dark, a little lighter and warmer at its foot,
   worked with a small round (upright strokes in the towers, level in the
   roofs), clipped to a silhouette built from a tabulated roofline (houses
   drawn at random as gable ends or broadsides, trees, two poplars, a Gothic
   west tower with corner pinnacles and a spire, nave with a ridge turret,
   a gate tower, a second church with a bell cap and lantern); a post mill
   on the far shore with four sails pulled out from the hub with a pointed
   round; belfry openings as four upright touches a step lighter.
4. **water**: the lagoon under the glow, level strokes of the sky mirrored
   (a step darker), the town's reflection as a soft dark; fused level with a
   small badger.
5. **land**: a thin brown dead color (clipped at the horizon), then the far
   meadows with a small filbert, the near ones with a larger, both level,
   the color field in value steps from a hazy mauve-gray at the horizon to a
   dark umber, with field bands widening toward us; then (after two hours
   on the clock) a grain of short near-level strokes a step off the paint
   under them, larger near.
6. **pools**: three flooded hollows, long level shapes laid out on the
   ground; the sky given back a step darker, the far shore's reflection as
   a dark band along their far side.
7. **grove**: three trees on the left, each crown several masses, worked in
   upright hatching; trunks.
8. **rise**: the knoll in one dark (clipped at the crest), strokes along its
   slope, its top taking a little cool sky light; after 90 minutes, a heath
   hatching a step darker with some rust and gray-green.
9. **grass**: tufts flicked up with a pointed round, clumped along the
   skyline so the edge is made of grass, patches down the slope, bigger near,
   mostly dark blades, a few catching the sky.
10. **figures**: a man in a long coat (the `wanderer` gesture set, both feet
    down) and a woman in a high-waisted dress and shawl (`woman`), backs to
    us, heads breaking the horizon; rim light on the side toward the glow.
11. **feet**: a few blades over their feet.
12. **glaze**: a weak even umber film deepening toward the edges (Friedrich
    to Carus), wandering slowly. Then the finish: varnish, cracks with a
    narrow opening, raking light.""")
s=s.replace("""## FRICTION

(written as I go)""","""## FRICTION

1. **Helpers above `main` stale every checkpoint.** My geometry functions
   (town roofline, crest, pools) sit above `main`, so every edit to them made
   the sky checkpoint stale and the next run cost the full 95 s sky again.
   Workaround: wrap each helper in `// ckpt: from <stage>` … `// ckpt: end`
   and adopt the old checkpoints once with `--stale-ok --ckpt`. It works, but
   it is bookkeeping a painter shouldn't have to know; and a crop run needs
   its own set of checkpoints (`_full_crop`), so "resume a crop from my
   whole-canvas checkpoint" is impossible (`--crop … --resume grass` just
   fails with no checkpoint).
2. **No way to change the brush on a preset.** `Handling` has no `tool()`
   builder; to paint a `detail()` handling with a smaller round I had to
   write a little extension trait that sets the public field. Every painter
   will want this.
3. **`Palette::only` panics on a missing tube**, and the 1820 palette has no
   "smalt" (it's retained only in the early palette). Cost one 36 s run.
   A list of available tube names in the panic message would help (it names
   only the missing one).
4. **A glaze veil of pale paint turns milky white.** I laid an evening haze
   over the town's foot with `glaze(0.75)` of a pale warm color at load 0.55:
   the houses came out as white snow-covered cottages. Lead white scatters,
   so a "glaze" of it is a body scumble; the preset's name promised a veil.
   Removed it; the haze now lives in the town's own color field (lighter,
   warmer at its foot).
5. **Unclipped strokes overshoot a horizon.** A land dead color with crossing
   strokes (unclipped, `cross 0.4`) threw dark lumps above the horizon all
   along it, like a row of whales. `clip(true)` fixed it, at the cost of a
   stencil edge; at the horizon that is acceptable because the lagoon and the
   far shore strip cover it.
6. **A mask's zero contour draws a line.** My pool mask was
   `smoothstep(-0.3, 0.4, inside)` and outside the pools "inside" was exactly
   0 along a line, which painted needle-thin tails out of both ends of every
   pool. Obvious once found; took a zoomed crop to see.
7. **Water in a ribbon is a road.** A winding stream of even width reads as a
   path however it's colored (I tried pale, then darker with a bank
   reflection, then broken into stretches). Not an engine fault exactly, but
   nothing in the tools helps a painter make narrow water read as water;
   long level pools did it at once.
8. **Picket hedges.** Hedges drawn as rows of small upright pointed strokes
   read as fences or palisades; lumpy bands painted level read as floating
   dark leaves when broken. I dropped hedges.
9. **Figure helpers' hands.** The `woman` gesture paints hands in the `skin`
   paint; a normal flesh tone is the lightest thing on a backlit figure and
   read as two white dots. Painted them dark.""")

# Craft notes from r14_p2 (evening over a flat country, a town on the horizon, two figures)

For the painters who come after. What I tried, what happened, and why I think it happened.

## Composition first, and fast

I had a whole picture on the canvas within the first quarter hour: every stage crude, but all of
them there. Almost everything I changed afterward was a matter of the whole, not the parts: the
foreground rise was a black slab that swallowed half the picture until I dropped it to a knoll on
the right; the meadows only had room to recede once the rise got out of their way; the figures'
heads only broke the horizon once the knoll was raised a few units. None of those could have been
judged in a part of the picture. Get the whole thing up crude, then look at it.

## A town on the horizon

**The spire carries it, as the notebook says.** A tall west tower with a spire, a second church
with a blunter cap and a row of roofs read as a town at once, even as a flat silhouette.

**Houses drawn as a repeated shape read as a row of igloos.** My first roofline used rounded bumps
for trees and similar gables for houses, evenly spaced. At full size it was a string of beads.
Mixing gable ends with broadside roofs, varying widths and heights, a couple of tall narrow
poplars and the odd lumpy tree broke the rhythm.

**Small true details make a silhouette believable.** Corner pinnacles where the spire meets the
tower, a ridge turret on the nave, a lantern on the second church's cap and, most of all, a few
narrow upright touches a step lighter where the belfry openings are. Those four touches did more
for the towers than anything else: the evening shows through them.

**Don't veil a backlit town with pale paint.** I laid a thin pale haze over the town's foot to make
it rise out of mist. Pale paint over dark is not a glaze: lead white scatters, and the houses came
out as white cottages in snow. Putting the haze into the town's own color (a little lighter and
warmer toward the foot) gave the air without the whitewash.

## Water in flat land

**A narrow stream of even width reads as a road.** I tried a winding stream through the meadows
three ways: pale, darker with the far bank reflected along it, and broken into stretches hidden by
banks. Each time it read as a path. The eye takes any band of constant width that winds through
land as something to walk on.

**Long level pools read as water at once.** Flooded hollows laid out on the ground, so they are
wide and very flat, the sky given back a step darker and the far shore's reflection as a dark band
along their far edge, were water from the first look. But their first edges were clean lens shapes
with needle points at the ends, which read as pasted on. Carrying the meadow paint back over the
shores in short level strokes (not a rim of a darker color, the meadow itself) sank them into the
grass. Don't let that shore pass eat a shallow pool: it takes a unit or so from every edge.

**A mask that is exactly zero on a line will paint that line.** My pools had needle-thin tails out
of both ends for a long time. The shape function was zero along a line outside each pool and the
mask's soft edge started below zero, so the line got half coverage. Any soft mask whose ramp
straddles zero will do this where the field is flat at zero.

## Meadows at dusk

**Hue alternation reads as camouflage.** Field bands alternating slightly greener and slightly
redder, plus the palette's per-pile jitter, gave a near meadow like a camouflage net. Halving the
hue swing and lowering the mixing jitter made it one brown earth with a grain in it. Value steps
toward the viewer did the recession; hue did nothing but make noise.

**Olive is what brown looks like next to a violet sky.** My first meadows were a neutral olive
brown by the numbers and read green in the picture. Shifting them toward red, and a mauve gray at
the horizon, made them read as earth at evening.

**A dark dead color for land has to stop at the horizon.** Crossing strokes of a land underpainting,
unclipped, threw dark lumps above the horizon along its whole length. The horizon is the one line
you can't let a stroke overshoot.

**A dry brush over dry paint laid slabs, not a broken scumble.** I wanted the flat meadows to catch
a little sky light, the way wet flat ground does at dusk, so I dragged a nearly empty brush of a
lighter tone level over the dry meadow. It laid flat opaque patches that read as snow or scattered
pale stones, even when the tone was barely lighter. It didn't break on the grain of the paint
under it; it broke stroke by stroke. I took it out.

## Sky

**Thin blue over a warm ground turns olive.** When I made the upper sky a cleaner blue, soft olive
blotches came up all over it, even with the stipple switched off. Where a thinned blue ran thin,
the orange-brown ground showed through and mixed with it optically to olive; the badger then
spread each hole into a soft cloud. A leaner and more covering dead color, a shade darker than the
sky, and a leaner lay-in cleared it. The warmer the ground, the more a blue sky needs body.

**Streaks laid in the wet sky sit in it, but they came out soft.** Clouds as part of the lay-in's
color, fused by the badger, never looked pasted on, as the notebook promised. But they lost their
lit undersides and read as soft smudges. I'd try laying the lit underside again, very thin, into
the still-wet sky right after the badger, before the stipple.

## Grass and the knoll

**Tufts scattered one by one are a sprinkle.** My first grass on the knoll was single small tufts
spread over the slope: an even sprinkle of V-marks. Patches of many tufts with bare ground between
them, and tufts bigger toward the bottom of the picture, turned the same number of strokes into a
slope with grass on it.

**Make the skyline out of grass.** Along the crest, tufts clumped hard (most of the crest bare, some
of it thick) broke the knoll's stencil edge into grass. Light blades only where the crest is
against the sky; against the dark meadow they were a row of pale ticks.

**The top of a mound takes the sky.** A dark knoll backlit by the glow is one dark, but its top
faces the sky and takes a little of its cool light. Lightening the top a touch, cooler, gave it
volume without any light from the glow side.

## Small things

**Aimed small light touches over a dark can come out far too pale.** A half tone for a tree's lit
side, aimed at a color a little lighter than the crown, dried nearly white and turned the tree into
a ghost. For small touches of a known paint over a known dark, mix by masstone, or test it on one
tree first.

**A figure helper's flesh is the lightest thing on a backlit figure.** Hands in a normal flesh tone
read as two white dots. Backlit, hands are as dark as the sleeves.

**A man in a long coat reads better than a man in a cape at this size.** The caped figure with a
beret was a bell with a hat; the long coat, shoulders and a bare head read as a man.

## Working method

- Stages cost what they cost: the sky took three quarters of every full render, everything else
  seconds. So I bundled sky changes together and changed the land freely.
- To find where an effect came from I stopped mid-stage by switching passes off in a crop. That
  was the fastest way to tell the lay-in's fault from the stipple's.
- What I would do differently: decide the value of the land against the sky first. My meadows were
  too light and too green for dusk in the first renders, and everything I put on them had to be
  rejudged after I darkened them.

I'm putting together the final summary now, listing render paths and the top five friction points, each backed by concrete receipts like specific code lines and file paths — for instance, confirming handling.rs has no tool() builder via grep results, and pinpointing the palette retain logic that drops "smalt" in palette.rs.

The friction points I'm settling on: stale helpers breaking checkpoint resumption for crops, missing mid-stage stop switches that made me hunt through env variables for the olive-blotch source, a milky scumble effect from lead white scattering instead of a true glaze, dry brush over dry paint producing slabs instead of broken texture, and small light touches over dark ground turning out far too pale. I want to keep the whole writeup tight.

(ᵔᴥᵔ) I painted an evening landscape in Friedrich's manner and wrote both sets of notes. The final whole render took about 133 s and came out byte-identical to one resumed from the "rise" stage (`cmp` reported IDENTICAL).

**The picture:** Two thirds of the canvas is sky. The sun has just set behind a small town on a flat coastal plain. The town is a silhouette: a Gothic west tower with a spire standing in the glow, a second church with a bell cap, a row of roofs and a windmill on the far shore. Below it is a lagoon, and flooded pools lie in brown meadows that get darker toward the viewer. On a dark knoll at the right, a man and a woman stand with their backs to us, their heads just breaking the horizon. Above the glow hangs a young crescent moon with its faint ashen light, and a few rooks fly home toward the town.

**Files:**
- `paintings/src/bin/r14_p2.rs`: the program
- `out/r14_p2_full.png`: the final render, 2400 × 1714
- `notes/r14_p2.md`: composition, stage-by-stage method, 12 friction items and my critique
- `notes/craft_r14_p2.md`: craft notes for the next painter

**My critique, briefly:** from across the room the sky is still a smooth, correct gradient, and the town reads more as cut paper than as distance. The notes cover the rest.

**Top five friction points:**
1. **Checkpoints go stale too easily.** Any edit to a helper function above `main` stales every checkpoint, so each tweak to the town's roofline or the knoll repainted the 95 s sky. The docs confirm that a stage's fingerprint covers "everything up to the closing brace of that block" (`paintings/src/run.rs`). My workaround was to wrap each helper in `// ckpt: from <stage>` … `// ckpt: end` and adopt old checkpoints with `--stale-ok --ckpt`. Also, a crop can't resume from the whole-canvas checkpoints; it needs its own set.
2. **There's no way to stop partway through a stage or skip one pass.** Soft olive blotches appeared all over the blue upper sky. To find the cause I had to add environment switches to my own program to turn the stipples off in a crop. The cause turned out to be thin blue over the warm ground, spread into blotches by the badger. A leaner, more covering dead color and lay-in cleared it.
3. **A "glaze" of pale paint turns milky.** `st.glaze(0.75)` with a pale warm color, meant as haze at the town's foot, turned the houses into white cottages in snow. Lead white scatters, so the veil was really an opaque layer. I moved the haze into the town's own color instead.
4. **Dry brush over dry paint lays slabs.** A nearly empty brush dragged lightly across the meadow laid flat, opaque patches that read as snow or scattered stones, even at +0.02 L. It didn't break up on the paint's grain. I removed the pass.
5. **Small light touches over a dark came out far too pale.** Touches aimed at `#554b45` over a tree crown dried to roughly `#7a7068` and turned the tree into a pale ghost. I removed them.

A small one to add: `Handling` has no `tool()` builder, so swapping a preset's brush needed a small extension trait in my program.
